mappings.note: Single substitution into W = F x s with force and displacement aligned - LO-2. No gravity, no energy form, so none of the LO-6 or LO-7 siblings apply.
P = W/t for a lamp. Calculation only, so C-2.6-LO-2 and not C-2.6-LO-1; this stem recurs three times in the chapter and each occurrence honestly carries the same single outcome.
Inverts PE = mgh for the height. LO-6 covers calculating with the potential-energy expression regardless of which symbol is unknown; LO-5 would require stating or deriving mgh instead.
W = F x s with the answer's emphasis on expressing it in joules. Arithmetically identical to L148 - a family that genuinely shares LO-2, since the unit clause alone does not pull it over to LO-1.
Velocity tripled gives a 1:9 KE ratio - the squared-velocity dependence worked through the expression, LO-6. The same outcome as the doubling items; only the factor differs.
Asks for WORK (LO-2) but the route is weight times height, i.e. the mgh expression (LO-6). Paired with L124; both straddle the work and potential-energy outcomes.

Two genuinely different halves: (a) gravity does zero work on an orbiting satellite, decided from the definition (LO-1), while (b) is a straight mgh work calculation (LO-2). One of the few items where the definition and the computation are both marked.
Scales a known PE by h/4 and 4h - proportional reasoning inside mgh, so LO-6. Not LO-5: the expression is used, never stated or derived.

Unlike the three bare lamp numericals, this one first asks for the DEFINITION of one watt, which is C-2.6-LO-1's unit clause; the calculation half is C-2.6-LO-2. That definition is the only thing separating it from L149 and L157.
Word-for-word the same lamp calculation as L149. Recorded with the identical single outcome rather than manufacturing a difference the item does not contain.
KE ratio 1:4 for v against 2v - the expression applied, LO-6. Same outcome as L152 and L160; the chapter simply repeats this comparison at several factors.

The stated goal is to SHOW work equals the change in kinetic energy, so the work-energy theorem (LO-3) leads; the derivation incidentally produces 1/2 mv^2 (LO-5). The mirror of S85, where deriving KE is the goal and the theorem is the tool.
Evaluates 1/2 mv^2 once and again for doubled velocity - two substitutions, one outcome. LO-6; the doubling observation is arithmetic here, not a stated relationship.
Solves the KE expression for the MASS and then re-evaluates for tripled velocity. Both directions of LO-6; no definition or theorem is invoked.
PE = mgh inverted for height, the same as L150 with different numbers. A near-duplicate pair that shares LO-6 honestly.
Same work, two different times, two powers - P = W/t computed twice (C-2.6-LO-2). The equal-work observation is implicit, so C-2.6-LO-1 is not added as it is in the stairs discussion items.
W = F x s for a plough, force along the furrow. LO-2; this sits with L148/L151 as the plain work-calculation family.
Work found as the DIFFERENCE of two kinetic energies, which is the work-energy theorem (LO-3) with LO-6 for evaluating them. Not LO-2: no force or distance is given, so W = F x s is unusable.
WEAK FIT on the second half. The lamp power is clean C-2.6-LO-2, but the heater part asks for energy over 10 hours expressed in kWh, and commercial energy units have no outcome in curriculum 82.

Stopping work equals the kinetic energy destroyed - work-energy theorem (LO-3) with the KE evaluation (LO-6). Same outcome pair as L165; accelerating and stopping are the same skill with opposite sign, and the frame does not separate them.
WEAK FIT. E = P x t for four devices (C-2.6-LO-2), but the item is graded on expressing the result in joules AND commercial units, and the kWh has no outcome in this frame.

POOR FIT. Solved entirely by the principle of moments about a fulcrum, including locating the scale's centre of gravity - no outcome states the moment principle. C-2.6-LO-3 covers the metre scale as a lever and C2.6 is the nearest thing to the force-times-arm relation.

POOR FIT. Parts (ii) and (iv) are velocity ratio, which has no code at all; part (iii) is a tension relation the frame never mentions. Only the pulley identification (LO-3) and the copy-and-mark-the-diagram task (C8.1) are genuinely covered.

Contrasts two named pulley types (LO-3) by the effort each demands, i.e. their mechanical advantage of 1 versus 2 (C2.6). The comparison of two machines is what earns LO-3 here, unlike the bare MA computations.

POOR FIT: of four sub-parts, only the work done by the effort maps cleanly (LO-2) and only MA touches C2.6. Velocity ratio and efficiency, which carry half the marks, have no outcome anywhere in curriculum 82.
